Scalded. Ordinary scalding is done in a kli sheini. Rokeach. See siman 447, seif 3, in Rama. It is possible that here the prohibition is based upon pouring from a kli rishon, and Mordechai called it a kli sheini only because the food was in a bowl. As a matter of law, if the liquid is sufficiently hot to cook upon contact, it is prohibited, for on Pesach chametz is treated stringently even regarding cold contact. Chok Yaakov.

Split. Since Rama did not gloss here, as he did above in seif 9, to prohibit even when the kernel is not split, perhaps here, because there is an additional doubt that it may have fallen afterward, we are not so stringent. Taz, however, writes that Rama follows his own position and prohibits even when it is not split whenever it softened. Here, however, where it was not split, it may be sold to a non-Jew because there is a double doubt: perhaps it did not become chametz, and perhaps it fell afterward. We are stringent only with a single doubt, as in seif 9. Chok Yaakov is lenient even in the case of seif 9 to permit sale to a non-Jew; see seif katan 18.

The chicken. We say that perhaps the wheat kernel was in the water at the time of scalding. The principle "it was found here and therefore was here" is applied only when the issue is movement from place to place or from one piece to another, as stated in seif katan 21. Within a single place, such as the scalding water, where the uncertainty is one of time and perhaps the kernel was already present earlier, we do not simply say that it fell only now. Chok Yaakov. The chicken's prior permitted status is weakened because it certainly was in water that may have become chametz. For this reason Rokeach prohibits a baked matzah in which a wheat kernel was found when it is unknown whether the kernel fermented while the matzah was still dough, but permits the other matzot.

Which prohibits. See what I wrote in seif katan 20.

It fell. Beit Yosef cites Rabbeinu Yerucham in the name of Rashba: if a wheat kernel was found in the utensil in which a chicken was rinsed, we say that it was there where it was found. Magen Avraham asks from Rashba's own ruling that if a wheat kernel is found in matzah, the entire dough is prohibited and we do not say that it fell only now. He concludes that Rashba's case is where the chicken was salted and afterward rinsed in a cold utensil, and a wheat kernel was then found in that utensil. We might have feared that the kernel had been inside the chicken while it was salted. Rashba teaches that we do not establish a prohibition from one place to another. Matzah is different because there the doubt can be from one time to another. Accordingly, there is no disagreement at all, unlike Rama's understanding. The statement that matzah is a case of doubt from one time to another must refer to a case in which some dough remained in his possession; otherwise it too would be from one place to another.

A doubt. Perhaps the kernel fell only now, and even if it had previously been in the chicken, perhaps it had already been digested. See Magen Avraham.

The chickens. Magen Avraham writes that this is not limited to chickens; the same applies to meat, since here we are discussing a whole wheat kernel for which digestion is not relevant. Erev Shabbos writes that chickens were mentioned as the greater novelty: although kernels are commonly found in them, the case still remains doubtful and we say perhaps the kernel fell afterward. There is also another possible doubt, namely that perhaps the halacha follows the view that cold contact imparts no flavor at all. Bach is stringent in these laws and challenges Rama. The primary ruling follows Rama, as Eliyah Zuta and Taz agree. Especially when the kernel is not split, there is plainly no reason for stringency as stated above. If it did not soften, one may be lenient in every case, as Bach and the later authorities agree.

Rabbinic. Rokeach writes that if a piece of chametz was found in a bucket of water and it was unknown whether the chametz was already present when water had earlier been taken for cooking, the cooked food was permitted while the water in the bucket was prohibited, because perhaps the non-Jew who brought the water placed the chametz there only then. Taz writes that the text evidently contains a scribal error and should read that the earlier water was drawn from a well. The meaning is that water was first drawn from the well for cooking, and afterward more water was drawn into the bucket and chametz was found in the bucket. It was unknown whether chametz had been in the well at the first drawing. The cooked food was permitted because the non-Jew may have placed the chametz into the bucket only during the later drawing.

In any event, if chametz soaked in cold water for 24 hours, all agree that it prohibits because soaking for 24 hours is equivalent to cooking. Bach and Maharshal write likewise.

An incident occurred in which a person placed a piece of matzah and a piece of chicken into his mouth and felt a wheat kernel. He removed the food and saw the kernel, but could not tell whether it had been in the matzah or the chicken. The chicken may be permitted through a double doubt: perhaps the kernel fell into the cold chicken only now, and even if it had been there earlier, perhaps it had been digested. If it had been in the matzah, it must have been there during baking, because if it fell on the cold matzah afterward it would roll off. Nevertheless, Magen Avraham inclines that the matzah too is permitted, because the prohibition of a minute amount on Pesach is rabbinic and we attribute the kernel leniently to the chicken. Still, a netilah must be removed from the place in the matzah from which the piece was taken.

He further writes that even if the other food was meat, it may be permitted, because we do not establish a prohibition from one place to another and may say that the kernel fell onto the cold meat only now. If, however, the meat had been lying in a bowl and he ate from that bowl, the meat is prohibited, because from one time to another we do establish the possibility that the kernel was already in the bowl when hot meat was poured into it, and a kli sheini is stringent on Pesach. Usually one can recognize whether the wheat kernel was cooked or baked together with the food. If the bowl was moved from place to place after cooling, however, we again attribute the matter leniently, because we do not establish a prohibition from one place to another.

Which was soaked. See Magen Avraham and Chok Yaakov.

(65) "Ben yomo." This refers to a utensil that underwent hagalah before chametz became prohibited. Otherwise one may not perform hagalah on a ben yomo utensil, as explained above in siman 452. The Mechaber specifies a ben yomo cauldron because if the cauldron were not ben yomo, even the hagalah water itself would be permitted on Pesach, since the hagalah took place before Pesach and the absorbed flavor was not ben yomo, as explained above in siman 451 and in siman 447, seif 5, in Rama. Know that if the hagalah itself was performed during Pesach, then even if the cauldron was not ben yomo the water in the well is prohibited according to Rama above, siman 447, seif 10.

(66) "And they descended," etc., during Pesach. Meaning that the water flowed into the well during Pesach, but the hagalah took place before Pesach. If the water also entered the well before Pesach, it became nullified in 60 in the well water. Some are stringent that even when there is 60 one should not initially use that water, since other water can easily be obtained. "It is forbidden to drink its water." If one nevertheless cooked with it, Pri Megadim writes that in a case of major financial loss one may permit the food because the hagalah took place before Pesach.

(67) "Because they became mixed." Meaning that even according to those who above permit cold contact because it imparts no flavor, here it is prohibited because the actual chametz substance became mixed into the water. If wheat kernels are found in a well on Pesach, the later authorities write that as far as possible one should avoid using that water even according to the lenient view regarding cold contact, lest the kernels remained soaked there for a full 24 hours. If no other water is available and a person's basic needs depend upon it, one may be lenient through a double doubt: perhaps the kernels fell in only now, and even if they fell more than 24 hours earlier, perhaps they did not split and soften until later, so they were not soaked for 24 hours after becoming chametz. We may also rely upon the authorities who hold that cold contact does not prohibit without 24-hour soaking. Regarding a slice of bread found in a well, see above, seif katan 62. One who draws water on Pesach from wells belonging to non-Jews, or from Jewish wells that were not guarded from chametz during the year, should strain the water through a clean cloth each time it is drawn.

Bach writes that one should say "and our descendants and the descendants of our descendants," because the Sages say that whenever a person, his son, and his son's son are Torah scholars, Torah will never cease from his offspring. It appears to me, however, that the word "our descendants" already means all who issue from our loins, and the Targum on Job 21 renders "and his descendants" as "sons and sons of sons." Therefore the established text should not be changed.

The writer. It appears that this applies specifically to one who writes sacred texts for himself as part of his learning and understands what he writes. A copyist who merely copies and does not seek to understand what he writes need not recite Birchot HaTorah, because this is not Torah study. Even regarding one who writes as part of his study the matter requires consideration, because at minimum writing is comparable to contemplation. Agudah concludes that this applies provided he is not writing ordinary letters, and Tashbetz writes likewise. The meaning must be that even if he happens to write Scriptural verses in ordinary correspondence, he need not recite the blessing.
Rambam, chapter 7 of Hilchot Tefillah. Re'em and Tur write that some versions read "to engage in words of Torah," and this is also the Ashkenazic and Polish text.

"One who rises early," etc., recites Birchot HaTorah. See Mishnah Berurah regarding the case where he went back to sleep afterward. The principal question is whether sleep by day or a second sleep at night creates a new interruption requiring another blessing. The authorities dispute this because Birchot HaTorah resemble Birchot HaMitzvot in some respects and Birchot HaShevach in others.

If one slept a fixed sleep by day, many authorities hold that he should recite Birchot HaTorah again upon rising, because a fixed sleep is a genuine interruption. Others disagree and hold that the morning blessing continues for the entire day until the next principal night's sleep. Since the matter concerns a doubtful blessing, the usual practice is not to recite a new blessing after a daytime sleep. One who wishes to satisfy all opinions should have in mind when reciting Ahavat Olam in the evening to discharge any renewed obligation and then study immediately afterward.

If one rose in the middle of the night, recited Birchot HaTorah, studied, and then returned to sleep until morning, there is a substantial dispute. Magen Avraham holds that the later sleep constitutes an interruption and requires a new blessing in the morning. Several later authorities disagree. Pri Chadash and others maintain that once he recited the blessing after his principal nighttime awakening, he need not repeat it. In practice the doubt should be avoided where possible by hearing the blessing from another person or by intending to be discharged through Ahavah Rabbah and studying immediately afterward.

The rule is different when the first awakening was merely temporary and the person clearly intended to return to sleep. In such a case it is preferable, where feasible, not to recite Birchot HaTorah until the final awakening. If he needs to study Torah during the temporary awakening, however, he must not study without a blessing, and he should recite it then. Whether he must repeat the blessing after returning to sleep remains subject to the dispute just mentioned.

The later authorities also discuss one who remained awake the entire night. Since he did not have the ordinary interruption of sleep, some hold that he should not recite a new Birchot HaTorah in the morning. Others hold that the obligation renews each day. The accepted practical method is to hear the blessings from someone who slept, answer Amen, and then study. If no such person is available, the various customs follow the rulings of the later authorities as explained in Mishnah Berurah.

All this concerns actual Torah study. Mere contemplation does not require a blessing according to the principal ruling, although writing Torah as part of learning may be different, as explained above.
notes: Fresh translation from Hebrew; long halachic discussion rendered conservatively from the complete case.

(44) "Women are also obligated." Although these are time-bound mitzvot, women are nevertheless obligated because they too were included in that miracle.

(45) "The mitzvot practiced," etc. Such as matzah, maror, and reciting the Haggadah.

Seif 6, "he washes his hands." Pesachim 115a-b.

"And he does not recite a blessing." See Tosafos there, beginning "Kol," etc., and what I wrote in siman 158, seif 4, that the primary halacha is that one recites al netilat yadayim for food dipped in liquid. See there.

"And he takes." The Mishnah states that one dips with chazeret, as explained above.

"Less than a kezayit." Since he takes it only as a recognition for the children, and one recites the first blessing even over less than a kezayit, as Tosafos writes in the second chapter of Sukkah in the name of the Yerushalmi and as explained at the beginning of the sixth chapter of Berachot. He should not take a full kezayit. See Taz.

"And he recites a blessing." Gemara there.

"And he does not recite an after-blessing." Meaning even if he ate a kezayit, as explained above. This follows from the Gemara, 115a, which indicates that the first blessing ultimately exempts it. See Rashbam 114b, beginning "Peshita," and Tosafos 115a, beginning "Vehadar," who dispute Rashbam and R' Yosef Tov Elem. Rosh, however, explains like Rashbam. Tosafos' question from 115b, that Haggadah and Hallel constitute an interruption, applies specifically to handwashing, not to the blessing, because even companions who changed place do not create an interruption where some companions remained. See Tosafos 102a, beginning "Ve'akru." Seder HaPesach writes that a practical difference between these explanations concerns the after-blessing. See also Tosafos 100b, at the end of "Yedei Yayin," and Rosh there.

"And he takes the matzah." As explained above. The middle matzah is specified in accordance with the law of placing a broken piece together with a whole loaf.

"And he places half." So that both matzah-eatings performed for the mitzvah come from the broken piece.

"And he raises." As the Gemara states that matzah requires raising. See Hagahot Maimoniyot.

"And he says in the language," etc. As Scripture states, "And you shall tell your son," etc.

"And afterward he instructs," etc. The Gemara there discusses why the table or seder plate is removed, and Tosafos explains the reason.
